articles.title_orig: Italy fines Meta $887M for accessing Android users’ photos
articles.title_zh: Italy fines Meta $887M for accessing Android users’ photos
articles.content_orig:
Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from users' phone galleries for them to post.
The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian users' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent.
The company has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately.
Meta plans to appeal and calls the fine "disproportionate", a spokesperson said in a statement reported by Reuters.
The app asks for gallery access via a single permission that covers the whole app and several functions with different purposes, the authority found. A general notice about enabling other features appears first, but it does not make it clear to users that they are also enabling gallery suggestions.
Fully granted, a permission like this lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive, usually on an ongoing basis. Neither the user nor the authority can check which information is actually used.
The authority found a breach of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which puts the EU's ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats a phone as part of a person's private life. Any access to what the phone stores, therefore, requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results.
The authority's order, set out in its press release , requires the company to:
If the company misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent.
Meta said in a statement quoted in a Reuters report that the feature works only after users give permission on their device, and that they can change that permission at any time in their settings.
The Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti, the Bolzano consumer protection group whose complaint started the investigation, published consumer advice on July 11, 2025. It told users to switch off the gallery suggestion settings in the app and to check what access and permissions the Facebook app has on their phone.
The investigation did not look at whether gallery content was used to train AI models. The company denies any such use. The authority may separately examine a newer feature, launched this year, that allows gallery content to be processed in the cloud.
The company had argued that Ireland's data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules do not provide a one-stop-shop mechanism.
The feature has been available since 2023. The investigation began in July 2025 and included the authority's own technical analysis.
The fine equals about 0.47% of the group's global revenue. In setting it, the authority weighed the large number of people involved, about 20 million Android users in Italy.
It also weighed how long the breach has lasted. The breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the app, and for those who have already granted permission, the authority said.
Other factors were a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation. Changes the company made after the complaint counted in its favor, though the authority judged them late and limited to people who update the app.

articles.title_orig: Trump to meet Xi and Putin in China
articles.title_zh: Trump to meet Xi and Putin in China
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

articles.title_orig: Apple Bets on Siri AI Apps as the Main Draw for Its Smart Glasses
articles.title_zh: Apple Bets on Siri AI Apps as the Main Draw for Its Smart Glasses
articles.content_orig:
Apple plans to unveil its first smart glasses at WWDC in June 2027 and begin shipping them before the end of the year, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman .
In the latest edition of his "Power On" newsletter , Gurman shared new details about the glasses' design, charging system, and Siri features.
Current prototypes of the glasses, internally code-named "N50," are reportedly slightly thinner than Meta's second-generation Ray-Bans. Some test units have oval camera openings integrated into the frame without protruding housings. A front light indicates use or charging, while Apple is experimenting with additional privacy features.
Apple is apparently developing multiple styles and colors, with an emphasis on materials, sensors, and audio quality. Employees have described the sound as "industry-leading," with the glasses supporting music playback, calls, and FaceTime audio.
Testers can also charge the prototype glasses while wearing them. A flat, three-pin magnetic connector, "roughly the size of a Tic Tac," attaches near the end of the left temple arm. Gurman said it remains unclear whether Apple will use this charging system in the shipping product.
The first model will not display augmented reality imagery. Wearers will interact through ‌Siri‌, which will use the cameras to answer questions about their surroundings.
Planned uses include identifying buildings, suggesting meals based on ingredients in a refrigerator, providing directions, and translating signs and conversations. Apple also intends to support calls, messages, iPhone notifications, calendars, standard and visual reminders, music controls, and smart home controls.
To support the glasses, developers will need to let ‌Siri‌ control specific features in their iPhone apps. Apple envisions tasks such as booking restaurant tables, requesting rides, ordering coffee, shopping, and purchasing movie tickets working on the device.
Developers will not need to create separate apps for the glasses. Their software will run on a paired iPhone, with the two devices working together to fulfill requests. Current plans require a recent iPhone model, with no Android support. The paired phone will compensate for the glasses' limited processing power and memory.
Wi-Fi will allow certain functions outside third-party apps to remain available without a nearby iPhone. Gurman suggested audio playback could theoretically continue over Wi-Fi, although the glasses will not function as a fully independent device.
Internal prototypes purportedly run a reduced version of visionOS 28 and contain a processor derived from older Apple Watch chips. Other custom components handle wireless connectivity and process images as the cameras capture them.
Apple began introducing the necessary ‌Siri‌ controls in this month's first iOS 27.3 beta, enabling more precise control of app actions. Originally demonstrated in 2024, the capability has been rebuilt using newer AI models. Apple plans to release support for its own apps in December, followed by third-party support in 2027.
Apple wants developers to prepare those integrations before the glasses arrive and continues to target a WWDC announcement next year. The company sees access to its existing app ecosystem as a major selling point against rival smart glasses.
The device will also overlap with camera-equipped AirPods, which remain scheduled for launch in late 2027 and will also provide ‌Siri‌ with information about the user's surroundings. The glasses should offer longer battery life and accommodate more sensors, with Apple seeing the potential for them to be worn throughout the day.
Work on the glasses started in the early 2020s, and Apple is said to have largely settled on the hardware. The remaining obstacles involve software and AI, which Gurman said are running late and could delay the planned 2027 launch.

articles.title_orig: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, Architect of Mexico’s Modern Drug Trade, Dies at 80
articles.title_zh: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, Architect of Mexico’s Modern Drug Trade, Dies at 80
articles.content_orig:
Updated: November 15, 2026 at 5:28p.m. EST
Published: November 15, 2026 at 4:47p.m. EST
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking, the “boss of bosses” who transformed the global cocaine trade, died Sunday aged 80, officials said.
The notorious drug kingpin died in a hospital where he had been transferred from prison two days earlier.
“After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on Nov. 15 at the medical facility” after “he suffered multiple organ failure,” according to a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.
One of the founders of the Guadalajara cartel, from which the Sinaloa cartel would later emerge, Felix Gallardo had been incarcerated since 1989.
He was a key player in establishing ties to Colombian drug traffickers and was convicted for the 1985 murder of an undercover agent working for the Drug Enforcement Agency, Enrique “Kiki” Camarena Salazar, which outraged the United States.

articles.title_orig: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.
There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."
Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.
Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.
"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.
A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.
At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.
International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.
That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.
In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.
He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".
"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.
"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.
At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.
He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.
In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.
And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."
Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.
At a noisy sports centre, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.
He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.
He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.
And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.
Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.
He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.
At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.
"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.
He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".
There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.
The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.
Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.
"These people have so much to offer," he said.
"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

articles.title_orig: Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
articles.title_zh: Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
articles.content_orig:
Estonia will close its border crossings with Russia, after an attack on an Estonian defence company that Tallinn blames on Moscow.
The foreign minister made the announcement on Sunday, after eight people were detained overnight in connection with an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
Estonian authorities said the attacks had been ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote on X, “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.
“Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia’s ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention.”
He did not specify how long the border closure would last.
A Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman told state news agency TASS that the plans were “yet another bout of aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia.”
Latvia’s Interior Minister Janis Dombrava thanked Estonia’s Internal Security Service on X, saying that several “Latvian citizens and non-citizens” were arrested.
“Since the collapse of the USSR, there have been people among us who are willing to commit serious crimes in Russia’s interests. We will continue our work to ensure that such people cannot endanger the lives of those who love Latvia and want to live in safety,” Dombrava wrote.
Estonia, a European Union and NATO member state and a strong ally of Ukraine , currently has three open border crossings with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula.
Marko Mihkelson, chairman of the Estonian Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, told Al Jazeera that the arrests demonstrated that Estonia was “prepared to respond swiftly to such attacks.”
“It is essential that Russia’s state-sponsored campaign of terror does not remain merely a matter of diplomatic protests, either in Estonia or among our allies elsewhere,” Mihkelson said.
“Russia is waging a shadow war to divide Europe and undermine support for Ukraine. European countries must respond with asymmetric measures of their own. Closing borders with Russia is one such measure.”

articles.content_orig:
ULA said an ‘anomaly’ led to its Vulcan vehicle failing to deliver its payload to orbit.
ULA said an ‘anomaly’ led to its Vulcan vehicle failing to deliver its payload to orbit.
United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon’s competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a small portion of the necessary satellites to challenge Starlink into orbit. Today’s launch was supposed to be the first of 38 flights Amazon purchased from ULA.
In a statement posted on X , ULA said, “Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.”
The company said it was currently unclear what caused the failure, but pledged transparency as it continues its investigation. Amazon projected confidence in its launch partner despite the failure, posting on X that, “ There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01. ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

articles.title_orig: F.D.A. Rejects Closely Watched Lung Cancer Drug From China
articles.title_zh: F.D.A. Rejects Closely Watched Lung Cancer Drug From China
articles.content_orig:
The immuno-oncology revolution will have to wait.
The FDA has issued a complete response letter to Summit Therapeutics, declining to approve the highly anticipated PD-1xVEGF bispecific ivonescimab for patients with previously treated, EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer.
The rejection derails the immediate U.S. launch of a drug class that many industry heavyweights believe could eventually dethrone Merck & Co.’s Keytruda.
Summit’s initial application targeted a niche, and as Leerink Partners analysts pointed out in a Nov. 5 note, the limitations of the clinical trial behind the application are not directly transferable to Summit’s broader development program for ivonescimab.
To industry watchers, the regulatory snub does not come as a total surprise. In their Nov. 5 note, Leerink analysts assigned Summit’s bid a 40% probability to approval. That’s because the phase 3 Harmoni trial underpinning Summit’s application failed to meet its overall survival (OS) endpoint, even as the FDA specifically demanded a statistically significant death reduction.
At the primary overall survival analysis of the global Harmoni trial last year, the OS hazard ratio was 0.98 in the Western subgroup, indicating no survival benefit for ivonescimab plus chemotherapy versus chemo alone at that time. Summit argued that the OS data in the Western cohort was too immature compared to the China cohort, and subsequent data cuts showed that Western results improved to 0.76 by June 2026, matching the result from the entire trial. The FDA, however, apparently decided to stick with its OS requirement.
In the CRL, the FDA noted that, without a statistically significant OS improvement, Summit has not established substantial evidence of effectiveness, and that a progression-free survival (PFS) benefit in the absence of a statistically significant OS does not support a positive benefit-risk profile in support of approval, according to Summit.
“We are disappointed for patients and their families awaiting additional treatment options in this setting,” Robert Duggan, chairman and co-CEO of Summit said in a Nov. 15 release.
Before FDA handed out the rejection, Summit had parted ways with its chief commercial officer Robert LaCaze and several senior commercial and marketing leaders who were tasked with building ivonescimab’s launch plan.
Meanwhile, back in China, where ivonescimab’s original developer, Akeso, is in charge, authorities granted the drug its first approval in May 2024 in the same indication of tyrosine kinase inhibitor-pretreated EGFR-mutated nonsquamous NSCLC. Then, the China-only Harmoni-A trial, part of which was merged into the global Harmoni trial, met its OS endpoint at the final analysis with a 26% death risk reduction.
Ivonescimab’s setback has narrowed its potential first-mover advantage as several pharma giants— including Merck —race to advance their own PD-(L)1xVEGF bispecifics.
Pfizer’s 3SBio-partnered tivunatamig (PF-08634404), BioNTech and Bristol Myers Squibb’s pumitamig , Merck’s MK-2010 and AbbVie’s ABBV-1480 are all getting pushed into global phase 3 trials.
Even in the second-line EGFR-mutated NSCLC space, ivonescimab’s absence means one less competitor for TROP2-directed antibody-drug conjugates such as AstraZeneca and Daiichi Sankyo’s Datroway and Merck’s Kelun-Biotech-partnered sac-TMT , as well as BMS’ dual-targeting EGFRxHER3 bispecific ADC, iza-bren .
Now, attention around the PD-(L)1xVEGF class is shifting to the all-important first-line NSCLC setting. As Leerink’s analysts noted, the real test for ivonescimab remains the upcoming readout from the Harmoni-3 trial in first-line NSCLC.
Summit scared investors in April, when a newly added interim analysis of the trial’s squamous cohort missed statistical significance on PFS. The squamous subgroup is now moving toward a final PFS analysis by the end of this year, and the nonsquamous group could report PFS data in the first half of 2027.
Despite the regulatory sting, Summit is far from defeated. Just weeks before the FDA’s decision, the biotech secured a $2 billion cash injection from AZ.
The company now has the financial firepower to fund additional trials for ivonescimab, and AZ plans to pair its sprawling ADC pipeline with the PD-1xVEGF drug, an approach that some considered the next-frontier in immuno-oncology.
“With five positive Phase III studies between Summit and Akeso, nothing changes with respect to our ever-growing belief in the opportunity for ivonescimab and our determination to advance ivonescimab’s development,” Duggan said. “Our mission remains to improve outcomes for patients facing significant unmet needs, which is work worth doing, and we will continue through our expansive clinical development program.”

articles.title_orig: Megaspeed Says Alice Huang Left Company in August 2025
articles.title_zh: Megaspeed Says Alice Huang Left Company in August 2025
articles.content_orig:
Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center company, said in a statement on Sunday that Alice Huang, a former executive at the center of what U.S. officials call a Chinese spy plot targeting the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, had left the company in August 2025.
The statement, which was reported by The Associated Press, was Megaspeed’s first to directly address the status of Ms. Huang since she became the focus of international scrutiny over her ties to Mr. Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday.
News of their relationship rocked Nvidia, the dominant maker of artificial intelligence chips, as well as the global technology sector and the U.S. government.
Last month, The New York Times reported that American officials had concluded Ms. Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset and had a close relationship with Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom and an adviser to President Trump.
Mr. Huang acknowledged last Sunday that he’d had an affair with Ms. Huang, and Nvidia’s board of directors said they had begun an investigation into his conduct . On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that he also had an extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him. articles.title_orig: Anthropic’s giant IPO puts the heat on OpenAI
articles.title_zh: Anthropic’s giant IPO puts the heat on OpenAI
articles.content_orig:
Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , the tech industry is under mounting strain.
Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.
With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon , whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.
Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus . It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google , though delivery won't start until 2028.
"The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it."
Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.
By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.
The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.
"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."
Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.
"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.
Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.
It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.
Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.
Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.
The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.
Google will be paying particularly close attention.
The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf , which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said .
"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.
Google didn't provide a comment.
One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.
"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."
Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America , Blackstone , Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion .
That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.
"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."

articles.title_orig: Intel Razor Lake reportedly gets 12 P-core-only die with bLLC on Intel 18A-P
articles.title_zh: Intel Razor Lake reportedly gets 12 P-core-only die with bLLC on Intel 18A-P
articles.content_orig:
A new Razor Lake leak reveals a 12+0+4 processor built on Intel 18A-P.
Please note that this post is tagged as a rumor .
Intel is reportedly preparing an unlocked Razor Lake desktop processor featuring 12 P-cores on a single compute die. According to hardware leaker Jaykihn, the processor will use Intel’s 18A-P manufacturing process and feature bLLC (Big Last Level Cache). This would be a different design from the other planned Razor Lake desktop processors, which reportedly use TSMC N2P.
Jaykihn reports that the processor has a 12+0+4 configuration, consisting of 12 performance cores, no standard efficiency cores and four low-power efficiency cores. The 12 P-cores reportedly use the Coyote Cove architecture, which Intel is also expected to introduce with Nova Lake.
The leaker clarified that this is a dedicated P-core-only compute die, rather than a hybrid design with disabled E-cores. He also confirmed that all 12 P-cores reside on a single die, rather than two compute tiles with six P-cores each. The processor is reportedly unlocked and includes bLLC, although its cache capacity has not been specified.
This replaces the previously-rumored locked 8+0+4 bLLC SKU.
— Jaykihn (@jaykihn0) November 15, 2026
This configuration replaces a previously rumored locked 8+0+4 Razor Lake processor with bLLC. Jaykihn also reports that the planned 125W 6+12+4 bLLC segment will no longer launch with Nova Lake and has instead been delayed to Razor Lake.
Jaykihn initially could not confirm which manufacturing process Intel would use for the 12 P-core design. He later updated his information, stating that the compute tile uses Intel 18A-P. This makes it an exception among the currently reported Razor Lake desktop compute tiles.
According to the same source, the remaining configurations use TSMC N2P. These include a 4+8 design with Coyote Cove (CYC) P-cores and an 8+16 design with Griffin Cove (GFC) P-cores. The latter reportedly comes in variants with and without bLLC.
Razor Lake is expected to succeed Nova Lake in 2028, it should launch as the Core Ultra 5000 series.

articles.title_orig: Bessent Says Nvidia Needs ‘Dramatic Shakeup’ With Huang Out
articles.title_zh: Bessent Says Nvidia Needs ‘Dramatic Shakeup’ With Huang Out
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings.
Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said in an interview on Fox News.
The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter.
Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter.
Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.
Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.
Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang.
"If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell.
Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales.
Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months.
"But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.
The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place.
Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners.
Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said.
There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information.
Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China . Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut.
Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

articles.title_orig: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Israel killed a senior Hamas commander involved in planning the October 7 attacks only two months after killing his predecessor, a fresh sign of how the Gaza conflict remains active despite a US-brokered ceasefire being in place.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) killed Samir Mahmoud Abu Younis, the commander of Hamas’ Rafah Brigade, in a strike in southern Gaza overnight Saturday, both Hamas and the IDF said.
Abu Younis, who was a long-time member of the brigade, had replaced Nael Abu Obeid, the previous commander who was killed in a strike in September. And Abu Obeid himself replaced Mohammad Sabaneh, another commander of the Rafah Brigade who was killed in May 2025.
The strike comes just days after an Israeli attack on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, in what the IDF said was an attempt to kill another Hamas commander.
In a statement, Hamas’ military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, acknowledged the death of Abu Younis, saying he had joined the brigade in 1991 and was “among the most prominent commanders who participated in planning and overseeing” the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.
“The IDF continues to eliminate Hamas leaders in Gaza, and another one joins his predecessors in the depths of hell,” said Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz. “The offensive policy that I am leading together with the Prime Minister and the IDF in Gaza will continue – until Gaza is demilitarized and there is no Hamas.”
The killing of Abu Younis underscores an emerging pattern in Gaza. Despite a nominal ceasefire that went into effect more than one year ago, Israel has continued to carry out strikes targeting members of Hamas, particularly senior commanders. But those commanders are quickly replaced as Hamas entrenches its own grip on power over the half of Gaza not occupied by Israel.
Meanwhile, the Board of Peace, a body created by the Trump administration with United Nations backing to oversee the Gaza ceasefire plan, remains sidelined, unable to make any substantive progress on the 20-point plan agreed to in October 2025.
On Friday, the board said it had held “very constructive discussions” with 17 countries about a civilian Gaza police force under the authority of a Palestinian technocratic committee that was supposed to run Gaza. But that committee has yet to enter the enclave, and an international security force meant to stabilize Gaza has yet to materialize.
The IDF strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza last week killed at least six people, including a doctor and a child, according to Palestinian officials. The strike hit the hospital’s surgery unit, killing Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira and a 13-year-old boy who was awaiting surgery. A total of 40 others were injured in the strike, including two doctors who were in critical condition, officials said.
In a statement, the IDF said it had targeted the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade, Muhammad Abu Ismail, as well as “additional terrorists who were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.” But when pressed on whether Abu Ismail was killed in the strike, the IDF did not answer.
Doctors Without Borders (Médicins Sans Frontières, or MSF) condemned the strike, saying: “It is unconscionable that patients and medical staff are once again being killed and injured inside a hospital, a place where lives should be saved, not taken.” MSF withdrew its own staff from the hospital in January because of the presence of armed men inside, as well as concerns over the hospital’s neutrality and management. “Under international humanitarian law, hospitals must be respected and protected,” MSF said.
The Board of Peace also urged both Israel and Hamas to uphold their commitments under the Comprehensive Peace Plan and protect civilians.
According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 1,600 people have been killed in near-daily Israeli strikes in Gaza since the ceasefire was signed one year ago.
The shattered territory also faces an unfolding humanitarian crisis ahead of the onset of winter. Last week, seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, where nearly two million Palestinians remain displaced.
In a joint statement Sunday, the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom said 150,000 tents and other vital supplies were being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza. They urged Israel to allow “immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access” and permit tents and dual-use items needed for humanitarian operations and early recovery into the enclave.
Israel said last week that more than 91,000 tents had entered Gaza ahead of winter, but it has refused to allow in the heavy equipment needed for large-scale clean-up and rubble removal efforts.
“The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms,” said Israel’s Coordinator for Government Activities in the Territories.
CNN’s Nic Robertson contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
articles.title_zh: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.
"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.
President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.
The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.
On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.
Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.
The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.
He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".
Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.
"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".
"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.
Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.
Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".
He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

articles.title_orig: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
articles.title_zh: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
articles.content_orig:
An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random.
The United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days. The timing is almost too coincidental to be a coincidence – coming on the heels of the removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO amidst an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, widespread recriminations about chip exports to China, and demands for tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China.
Could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S. infrastructure? It’s too early to know for sure, but the country deserves far more transparent answers than we have received so far.
At 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday , November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every departing flight in America, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the third nationwide ground stop ever ordered. The first came on Sept. 11, 2001; the second more than 20 years later, on Jan. 11, 2023.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would say only that “a communication issue” had struck every one of the 22 centers that guide planes across the country, and that technicians were investigating. A subsequent press conference by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did little to reassure anyone, with no answers about what happened and little reassurance that it would be fixable anytime soon, with airports sending travelers home and communicating that flight cancellations would persist for many hours at a minimum, if not days.
It was the second time in two days that critical infrastructure the country cannot function without simply stopped, potentially for very nefarious reasons. The day before, Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot went dark in 74 countries and stayed down for hours. Both blackouts struck within a day-and-a-half of the most damaging China espionage story in years.
The last nationwide ground stop, in 2023, lasted about 90 minutes and still delayed more than 10,000 flights and canceled 1,300 . Friday’s lasted hours with no resolution imminent on the horizon. At the four-hour point of this latest ground stop, 10,243 flights were already delayed and 3,234 cancelled, with flights grounded not only at single regional airports but across the entire nation, suggesting systemic breakdowns rather than localized issues.
Microsoft’s failure began at 11:17 a.m. ET on Thursday and spread across 19 Microsoft 365 services . Within an hour, complaints about Outlook were running at more than 2,000 times their normal level . Microsoft counts more than 450 million paid commercial seats , with many millions of those users locked out entirely from their inboxes and other critical services.
The casualty list reads like a roll call of essential services: the U.S. House of Representatives was substantively incapacitated; a federal appeals court that could not send or receive email; Britain’s Parliament and its National Health Service, where the failure threatened patients’ prescriptions; Australia’s spy agency and federal police were sent offline as well.
When a botched CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines in 2024, the Fortune 500 alone lost an estimated $5.4 billion . One risk adviser already puts Microsoft’s bill in the billions for Australia alone , not to mention the lost economic value in the U.S. or the rest of the world. This was the first time in history so many users were locked out for so long – with shifting and unsatisfactory explanations. Similarly, this is the first time in global aviation history where there has been a nationwide ground stop with no satisfactory, clear explanation and immediate fix.
Microsoft wrote the playbook for false comfort. For a full day it insisted there was “no indication” of malicious activity while its own bulletins showed it did not know what had broken. If it did not know for sure, then how could they know for sure there was no indication of anything malicious amidst shifting explanations?
First it blamed elevated load, then servers that had unexpectedly dropped out . It found no recent change that lined up with the failure. Hours later, it was rolling back a network change that did . Early Friday, engineers were still trying to “pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx.”
Only on Friday afternoon did Microsoft name a culprit : a flaw introduced during a network capacity upgrade, “not related to cyber.” That sequence is as nonsensical as it is falsely reassuring. No patient would trust a doctor who swears it is not an infection before he can diagnose the fever. You cannot rule out what you cannot yet explain, and nobody can feel particularly reassured from this disturbing sequence of events and shifting explanations.
On Thursday morning, Nvidia, whose board failures we dissected in Fortune this week , announced the resignation of Jensen Huang , the chip industry’s loudest advocate for selling to China, after he admitted an affair with a businesswoman U.S. officials suspect of spying for Beijing . Beijing has been vocal in calling it a smear amidst a rapid escalation of U.S.-China tensions. Lawmakers in both parties are demanding testimony and tighter export controls . Within three hours, inboxes went dark from Capitol Hill to Canberra. A day later, planes stopped and were grounded.
Could that really be a coincidence?
Perhaps we are being too conspiratorial, but there is a certain uncanny resemblance to Beijing’s favorite playbook, which is to divert from negative news stories by shutting down internet services and diverting public attention.
For example, in 2011, a petition to free Ai Weiwei got Change.org knocked offline . In 2012, exposés of the family fortunes of Xi Jinping and Wen Jiabao got Bloomberg and The New York Times blocked in China and targeted by hackers . In 2014, as Hong Kong marched for democracy, a newspaper and a voting site were buried under one of the largest attacks the internet had ever seen . In 2015, China’s “Great Cannon” hammered GitHub for days for hosting banned news. In 2019, Telegram and the LIHKG forum were swamped as Hong Kong marched again. In 2022, news of the zero-COVID protests on Twitter drowned in a deluge of spam . Maybe this pattern of untimely hacks was merely a coincidence – or could it have been more than coincidence?
Microsoft knows this adversary better than anyone. Hackers tied to Beijing tore through its customers’ Exchange servers in 2021 and stole some 60,000 State Department emails through its cloud in 2023, a breach a federal review board blamed on a “cascade of security failures” at Microsoft. Just three weeks ago, Microsoft itself said a China-aligned group had turned AI agents loose on more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 customers .
Whatever the cause, the lesson is identical. Some cyber experts are warning about potentially economically destabilizing cyberattacks, with researchers warning that AI-enabled hacking is spreading like a virus: attacks on previously unknown flaws have roughly doubled since capable open-source models arrived.
U.S. agencies say China’s Volt Typhoon hackers have already burrowed into American communications, transportation, energy and water networks , in some cases for five years, positioning themselves to disrupt them. They sat inside one small Massachusetts electric and water utility for more than 300 days . If the inbox and the skies can go dark on consecutive days, why not the grid, or the tap? Is it time for every business and household to buy storage batteries, water tanks, MREs and porta potties?
Of course, regardless of whether this was a Chinese or foreign malevolent actor attack, or whether it was merely the coincidental degradation of antiquated and outdated infrastructure systems, all of this takes place against the backdrop of the substantive hollowing out of U.S. government cou

The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.
"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."
Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.
"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.
Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.
It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.
Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.
Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.
The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.
Google will be paying particularly close attention.
The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf , which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said .
"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.
Google didn't provide a comment.
One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.
"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."
Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America , Blackstone , Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion .
That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.
"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."

articles.title_orig: Foreign leaders look beyond Trump on his Asian meeting spree
articles.title_zh: Foreign leaders look beyond Trump on his Asian meeting spree
articles.content_orig:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings
World leaders will fly in to Asia for back-to-back high-level summits this week against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections .
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy .
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.
“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”
Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines , starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.
While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.
Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea , where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.
The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.
For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.
Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.
Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.
“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.
Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.
Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas . Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.
A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore .
Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration . Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

articles.title_zh: Israel Kidnapped Iranian Generals in Flawed Hunt for a Missing Airman
articles.content_orig:
At a protest in 2025 in Tel Aviv, supporters of Israeli hostages held captive by Hamas held pictures of the hostages and of Ron Arad, who has been missing since 1986. Credit... Itai Ron/Reuters
By Adam Goldman Ronen Bergman Farnaz Fassihi and Hwaida Saad
Ronen Bergman, Farnaz Fassihi, Adam Goldman and Hwaida Saad have spent years investigating the disappearance of the Israeli airman Ron Arad.
Gen. Abdullah Saberi, an Iranian commander, stepped out for a jog early one morning in an upscale diplomatic quarter of Syria’s capital. Israeli intelligence officers waited nearby. Posing as movers, they had slipped past the neighborhood’s security checkpoints.
As he headed for a nearby park, General Saberi passed two men who carried an oversize refrigerator box. In a flash, the men restrained the general, drugged him, threw the box over his head, shoved him into a white van and left as if nothing had happened.
He was whisked to Israel for interrogation, according to numerous officials in the Middle East, including senior Iranian officials close to General Saberi and a Syrian official who reviewed video of the September 2021 kidnapping.
As a veteran of Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, General Saberi knew many secrets. But his interrogators were interested in only one.
What did he know about Ron Arad?
Mr. Arad, an Israeli airman, vanished decades ago, and the Israeli military says he is the only service member classified as missing in action. The government’s long search for him has captivated the public and has come to symbolize Israel’s commitment, rooted in Jewish tradition , to bringing its soldiers home, dead or alive. Articles, books and documentaries have been produced about the hunt for Mr. Arad.
The Israeli government was so determined to find him that, even four decades after his disappearance, it took the risk of kidnapping General Saberi in the shadow of his own embassy.

articles.title_orig: 'The Ultimate Gaming Machine' - Xbox Reveals Tons Of New Project Helix Information
articles.title_zh: 'The Ultimate Gaming Machine' - Xbox Reveals Tons Of New Project Helix Information
articles.content_orig:
As part of Xbox's 25th anniversary celebrations today, we've been treated to a new digital version of a magazine that was given out at Seattle FanFest earlier this week, available to read in full over on the official Xbox Wire website .
The bit that's getting most attention concerns Xbox Project Helix - the new next-gen console that's currently in the works over at Xbox HQ. The brand's VP of Next Generation, Jason Ronald, shares tons of new information across four pages in the magazine, helping to give us a better idea of what to expect from the upcoming console.
There's one section in particular that's getting all the interest on social media right now, where he clarifies that Project Helix is definitely a console that can play PC games, and definitely not a PC that happens to play console games.
"We're very clear on the design goal: Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games. The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customizability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."
Beyond this, Ronald talks in depth about loads of other aspects of what they're aiming for with Project Helix, and as mentioned, there's so much detail that it spreads across four pages of the magazine.
In the interest of highlighting as much as possible though, we thought we'd transcribe all of most notable quotes from the magazine down below, whereas you can read the added context inside of the magazine article itself.
Here are more of the key bits from the magazine article:
"When we think about Project Helix, it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine - one that removes all barriers of play that have historically existed. My entire library is accessible to me. I'm able to bring four generations of my Xbox library and progression with me and have it available instantly. And we remove the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games."
"We don't think the next generation is defined by 8K or 240 hertz, or some of the traditional metrics - it's really about gameplay innovation. It's about deeper immersion. It is about leveraging new technical advancements such as neural rendering, to deliver a new level of visual fidelity in more efficient and innovative ways. It's about new kinds of games and new game experiences that we haven't been able to do before. What excites me about the future is the idea of entirely new types of games that have never been possible before, delivered through all the innovation in the silicon and the hardware and the platform that we're delivering."
"When I think about what makes a console magical, it's that it just makes my games instantly accessible and ready to play in an instant. I don't have to worry about updating my operating system, updating drivers, configuring different settings - things like that. The hardware and the experience is entirely designed around playing games."
"The very first next-generation conversations we had were with all of our first-party studios. That was absolutely foundational to the design of what we've done with Project Helix - talking about where they saw the future of game design going, where they saw the future of their franchises going, and what was constraining their creative ambition."
"With Xbox One, I think we got so focused on expanding our aperture that we lost sight of what truly is magical, which is players, developers, and the games that they love. We have to build the best platform for game developers to deliver their creative vision."
"The other thing, and I think this is something that is unique about Xbox, is we have to be connected to the community. A lot of the features that people have come to love and expect from Xbox have actually been driven directly by community feedback. I think that's really core to the soul of who Xbox is, because if you're in touch with your player base, you never go wrong if you focus on what their needs are."
"It's definitely a challenging time, but as a system and a platform designer, it's also one of the most exciting times, because we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also continuing to make things accessible and affordable."
"This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering, because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower, additional memory, and things like that. I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last 10 years."
"The ROG Xbox Ally was really an opportunity for us to learn alongside our player base with a lot of these concepts and the ideas that we had: being able to play libraries from across multiple different storefronts, understanding how PC games and console games can show up together in a unified library. The feedback that we've gotten from players has fundamentally informed and altered our plans of how it actually shows up in a future console. Players shared where we met the mark and areas we needed to improve or approach differently. So absolutely, we view the Ally as a precursor to what we're doing with Helix - but it's informed by a lot of the design concepts we have for Helix."
Sorry for the wall of quotes, but we thought you might find all of this pretty interesting! It's not even the full extent of what Ronald had to say, as he also touched on the importance of game preservation to the Xbox platform in general, as well as how Project Helix will seemingly have a bespoke UI, but one that still feels familiar to Xbox fans.
Of course, we're still waiting on concrete details about what Helix will look like, how much it'll cost, how significant the PC integration will be, and loads of other things that will give us a much better picture of how it'll shape up.
It seems like we won't be getting that this year though, and if rumours are to be believed, Xbox might even be releasing a first-party handheld in 2027 before the Project Helix console in 2028 . Who knows... plans can always change.
For now, let us know what you think about this latest info on Xbox Project Helix down below, and we definitely recommend reading the full Xbox 25th anniversary magazine for yourself - we wish we could buy one to be honest!

articles.title_orig: Viktor Orbán’s party reels from $20mn hidden cash discovery
articles.title_zh: Viktor Orbán’s party reels from $20mn hidden cash discovery
articles.content_orig:
Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor Orbán, authorities have said.
Miklós Seszták, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.
On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".
Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into Seszták, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.
The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said.
The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the Orbán rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".
Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many Orbán-era policies since entering office.
Allegations of corruption and cronyism have long dogged Orbán, who during the course of his tenure turned Hungary into what the EU characterised as an "electoral autocracy".
His government faced accusations of offering lucrative government projects to allies. Orbán has strongly denied the claims.
Two of his former ministers, including Seszták, and the former central bank chief Gyorgy Matolcsy have been under arrest since September over accusations of graft in separate investigations. They all deny wrongdoing.
On Monday, Hungarian authorities also detained Orbán's brother and three others as part of a people-smuggling case.
The former prime minister ​dismissed it as political revenge, saying: "In this dirty game, ​the aim is the elimination of the political opponent and the establishment of a one-party system.
"I am the target, my younger brother is just a tool."
