articles.title_orig: Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending
articles.title_zh: Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending
articles.content_orig:
Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”
That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project , an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra . If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.
To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”
Bustillos told me that these issues have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself, for example when Tal Levin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”
“AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”
The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.
Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”
This is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.
“E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”
In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”
So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.
Flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries .
The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl, and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.
Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).
With Phoenix, newsletter writers (starting with those who use Ghost, with support for additional newsletter platforms coming in the future) will be able to offer subscriptions to libraries, similar to the way libraries can subscribe to newspapers and magazines. Once it’s set up, Phoenix will automatically convert whichever newsletter posts the writer wants into EPUB documents, which are then sent to libraries for digital lending.
Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Raganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.
“We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she said. “Those things go hand in hand.”
Flaming Hydra seeks to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project , with the campaign ending on November 27.

Yemeni forces fighting for the internationally recognized Saudi-backed government said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategic Bab el Mandeb strait, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control.
The government’s retreat ​from the Bab el Mandeb area hands the Houthis greater leverage over the maritime choke point, creating ‌a potent pressure point on global shipping while Iran continues to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.
This dual squeeze would further isolate Gulf oil producers from their main shipping routes.
The Bab el Mandeb strait is one ​of the world’s most important and busiest routes for global seaborne commodity and goods shipments, particularly ​from Asia to Europe via Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The southern Yemeni forces said they were ⁠redeploying toward Aden, where the government is based, as the Houthis — who control much of the north, ​including the capital Sanaa and Yemen’s most populous areas — increase pressure on the southern areas still under government control.
“The Southern ​Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the southern forces said in a statement.
“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the ​capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats.”
Government ​forces launched a military campaign in October to recapture the strategic coastal areas from the powerful militia, which had pushed south ‌in September ⁠in an attempt to seize control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast. The lightning offensive brought the Houthis within reach of Bab el Mandeb.
The escalation in fighting, which broke a 2022 U.N.-brokered truce, became another volatile front in the wider U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, as the Houthis continue to launch attacks on Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ​ally and the world’s biggest ​crude exporter.
Houthi attacks on ⁠the kingdom, which had enjoyed relative calm during the early months of the 9-month-old Iran war, have disrupted flights and oil supplies as the Houthis struck Saudi ​ports, airports and facilities of state oil company Saudi Aramco — including the kingdom’s Red Sea oil ​export hub ⁠of Yanbu.
In response, Saudi Arabia struck Houthi targets in Yemen, a country mired in civil war since 2014, when the Houthis pushed the government south. Impoverished Yemen has been grappling with one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
Fighting ⁠is intensifying ​around the western region of Taiz, with humanitarian conditions worsening. The ​city, which hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen by the latest fighting, remains besieged. Aid supplies are unable to ​enter, and civilians are unable to leave.

articles.title_orig: Windows 11 “SignDrop” Zero-Day Exploit Turns Microsoft’s Own Security Fix Against Itself, Grants SYSTEM Privileges
articles.title_zh: Windows 11 “SignDrop” Zero-Day Exploit Turns Microsoft’s Own Security Fix Against Itself, Grants SYSTEM Privileges
articles.content_orig:
A newly disclosed Windows zero-day vulnerability, dubbed SignDrop, could allow attackers with standard user privileges to gain full SYSTEM access by exploiting a security mechanism Microsoft introduced last year. Ironically, the affected component was specifically designed to prevent similar privilege-escalation attacks.
Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri , also known as Nightmare Eclipse or MSNightmare , published the SignDrop proof-of-concept (PoC) on GitHub on November 10, 2026 . The exploit targets Microsoft's Common Log File System (CLFS) driver, which handles logging operations for Windows applications and system services .
Microsoft introduced CLFS authentication hardening in October 2025 to address longstanding security vulnerabilities. The mitigation uses cryptographic authentication codes to verify log file integrity before the driver processes their contents .
However, Naceri discovered that the authentication mechanism itself can be manipulated into creating files with elevated privileges .
Specifically, the vulnerability affects how the clfs.sys driver creates accompanying .cnpf authentication files . An attacker can prepare a specially crafted log file and subsequently force a privileged Windows process, such as Microsoft Defender, to open it .
Through this interaction, CLFS can create an authentication file using SYSTEM privileges while retaining access permissions inherited from the attacker-controlled file. Combined with additional manipulation, this allows an ordinary user to escalate privileges .
The researcher also claims that the technique could bypass antivirus and endpoint detection and response (EDR) tamper protection , since the privileged file operations appear to originate from legitimate security processes.
Independent cybersecurity researchers at Cyderes successfully reproduced the exploit and obtained a SYSTEM-level command shell , confirming that the technique works under certain conditions.
Naceri tested SignDrop against Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental , estimating that approximately 80% of Windows installations could be vulnerable . However, this figure remains unverified, and independent researchers have reported compatibility and reliability limitations .
Users can inspect the following Windows Registry location to determine whether the affected CLFS authentication mechanism is enabled:
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode
According to Microsoft's documentation, a value of 0 (enforcement mode) or 1 (learning mode) indicates an active mitigation and a potentially vulnerable configuration . However, this alone does not guarantee that the exploit will succeed .
Importantly, users should not disable CLFS authentication as a workaround, since doing so could expose their computers to older memory-corruption vulnerabilities .
Microsoft has acknowledged the reports and is investigating the vulnerability . In a statement provided to SecurityWeek , the company said Microsoft Defender can detect and block exploitation attempts, adding that it has found no evidence of active exploitation in the wild .
At the time of writing, SignDrop has not received an official CVE designation or dedicated security patch . Users should continue installing Windows and Defender security updates while awaiting further guidance from Microsoft.

articles.title_orig: It’s not just an affair. Nvidia’s bigger issue could be chip smuggling.
articles.title_zh: It’s not just an affair. Nvidia’s bigger issue could be chip smuggling.
articles.content_orig:
Headquartered in a curved glass skyscraper that boasts commanding views over Singapore’s Marina Bay district, Megaspeed International is just the type of fast-growing tech start-up that Asia’s wealthy city-state has been keen to attract.
In three years, the corporate entity has gone from an inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US.
But its rapid rise has also propelled it to the center of an alleged spy scandal that’s now engulfing Nvidia , the $4 trillion company behind the world’s most advanced chips.
At the same time, suspicions that Megaspeed may be exploiting a loophole in US export controls is exacerbating a rift within the US government on how to best keep China from accessing its most sensitive technologies.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to having an affair. Congress has also called on him to testify behind closed doors about his romantic relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, whom US officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Beijing has said the claim is a “groundless” attempt to smear China.
Also known as Huang Le , the 43-year-old Chinese executive played an integral role in establishing Megaspeed, according to corporate documents and media reports. CNN has made continued efforts to reach her for comment.
But as Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia, it came under the scrutiny of the Singaporean government, as well as US officials concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers.
“Chips are the absolute ground-zero of all other technology,” said Alex Capri, a senior lecturer in the business school at the National University of Singapore. “The appetite for Nvidia’s chips in China is absolutely insatiable… Nvidia chips are still far and away the best.”
But US export controls have fettered Chinese access to its most advanced semiconductor technology, spawning a shadow industry of complex transactions, shell companies and chip smuggling – of which Megaspeed is now under suspicion by US authorities and lawmakers of helping enable.
Nvidia’s CEO is out after 33 years. What’s next?
On Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong said in a statement the company has cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce and has retained a US law firm to independently verify its compliance with export controls.
“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously. Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government,” the statement said.
In a new statement on Sunday, Megaspeed said that Huang left the company on August 30, 2025, and currently holds no role there.
“Megaspeed is aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence,” the statement said.
In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia’s most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China’s tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.
US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those.
Incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, the company’s name changed to Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became a director through November of that year. Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia.
Capri, who also wrote the book, “Techno-Nationalism: How It’s Reshaping Trade, Geopolitics and Society,” said Megaspeed’s business model, in which it builds data centers and rents out its computing services, gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips.
“If you put me on the restricted list to drive a Ferrari, and I say ‘Okay, well I can’t buy a Ferrari, I can’t import a Ferrari, but I can just go to a car dealership and rent a Ferrari,’ right? And do whatever I want with the Ferrari,” he said. “That’s an issue. It’s the car dealership that you have to control.”
Corporate filings show connections between subsidiary entities of Megaspeed and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, including the pledging of collateral. CNN has sought comment from Alibaba.
In other cases, Chinese buyers have been able to procure sensitive components of their own, often done through a web of ghost corporations and brokers through which the chips – sometimes concealed in other electronics or containers – can reach end users in China, experts said.
Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year.
“This is a pipeline that has developed that benefits from the fact that there is minimal scrutiny on US air data, that you can bring things into Singapore, Malaysia, Central and Southeast Asia and then move those goods, sometimes through Thailand, into China,” trade data investigator William George told CNN.
“It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks,” he said.
Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company’s server purchases and their final destinations.
In a statement, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence Huang that had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information “to downplay her role” at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.
The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws.
A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.
Jensen Huang, who has accompanied US President Donald Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, has lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue.
However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well.
They include Northwestern Polytechnical University, based in Xi’an, the capital of China’s Shaanxi province, one of the nation’s leading universities with military ties, known collectively as the “Seven Sons of National Defense.”
Northwestern Polytechnical University has been on the US Department of Commerce’s Entity List since 2001, yet it bought four H200 chips last month for $250,000, according to procurement records published on its own website that have since been deleted.
Northwestern Polytechnical University did not respond to a phone call from CNN seeking comment.
Despite investigation by the US, Megaspeed has not been labeled a national security threat or subject to limitations on chip purchases — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that led to a confrontation by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers, whose party recently won control of the House and Senate, are calling for greater oversight for US exports of advanced chips, days before Trump’s due to meet Xi for the third time this year in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 physical copies have no discs, and some apparently have no download codes either
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 physical copies have no discs, and some apparently have no download codes either
articles.content_orig:
Some GTA 6 buyers are opening their physical copies only to find no game disc or download code.
Rockstar has already decided that GTA 6 doesn’t need a physical disc, even when customers buy the physical version. Instead, players receive a plastic box with a digital download code printed inside. Apparently, even that is asking too much. Some buyers are now reporting that their copies arrived without a code, leaving them with an empty game case and a poster.
Reports have appeared on Reddit and X showing GTA 6 retail boxes with blank areas where the redemption code should have been printed. One buyer who purchased the game from Best Buy shared photos of the packaging, showing a gray strip but no visible code. Other customers have reported similar problems with PlayStation 5 and Xbox copies.
Where is my code? by u/Gahaman_214 in RockstarGames
The situation is made worse by the fact that some buyers have struggled to obtain replacements. According to customer reports, Rockstar support has closed tickets without resolving the problem, while at least one retailer initially refused a refund. Some affected customers have since received replacement copies. It is unclear how many boxes are affected or whether this is a printing error.
This follows another GTA 6 packaging controversy from earlier this week. Some players discovered that a flashlight could reportedly reveal download codes through certain sealed cases. The method appears to work only under specific conditions and has not been confirmed to result in code theft. Now we have the opposite problem: customers opening their boxes and discovering there is no code to reveal in the first place.
Puedes imaginar la ilusión de recibir el GTA VI después de reservarlo hace semanas y que te llegue sin el código. (No es un código que se raspa literalmente viene impreso así) @SoyAlexWhite #rockstargames #playstation #GTA6 #gtaiv pic.twitter.com/eXfEsGkB1a
— McKuin (@MrMckuin) November 13, 2026
Rockstar began shipping the $79.99 code-in-box edition on November 12, ahead of the game’s November 19 release. The company has not publicly explained the reported missing codes. Removing the disc was already an unpopular decision among physical game collectors. For some GTA 6 buyers, however, the physical edition has apparently become exactly that: a physical box, without the game.
At least these copies have one thing in common with the PC version of GTA 6: neither can be played.

articles.title_zh: US and allies sign accord to protect AI supply chains from China
articles.content_orig:
Americans are anxious about artificial intelligence . In the midterm elections , they voted to slow down its expansion. Forty local ballot measures in 10 states promise to tighten restrictions on data-center construction, with overwhelming public support. Measures to limit development of data centers won more than 70% of the vote in 30 of these electoral contests. A 2026 survey by Pew Research Center found that about 52% of Americans were more concerned than excited about the growing use of AI in daily life, up from 37% in 2021. Only 9% were more excited than concerned, and roughly six in ten said they wanted more control over how AI is used in their lives.
The sources of anxiety about AI are many: the safety of increasingly powerful systems and the ability to control them; the fear of job displacement; surveillance and the loss of privacy; a rising tide of misinformation and deep fakes; the enormous amounts of electricity and water that the data centers consume; and the concentration of wealth and power in a handful of companies that own the frontier AI models.
Until now, anxiety about the role of AI in geopolitical competition has largely been confined to policy circles. But the possibility that Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday, may have been compromised in a potential espionage scandal has brought that anxiety into the broader public sphere, fueling a frenzy over AI and the competition between the United States and China.
China is at the center of arguably two of the world’s most consequential economic and political developments: its dominance in global trade and its formidable AI capabilities. China and America are AI superpowers, but their strengths differ. America leads in computing power, thanks largely to Nvidia’s advanced chips. China is catching up fast in AI models. The economic and geopolitical implications of this competition are enormous.
There is another dimension to this competition: the economic effects of China’s trade dominance and the rising role of AI in the economy could reinforce each other and produce greater impact than either would have alone. China’s trade dominance is well-known. Two decades earlier, the economists David H. Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon H. Hanson gave that anxiety a name when they coined the term “ China Shock ” to describe the impact of the massive increase in Chinese exports to the U.S. in the early 2000s. The surge contributed to a sharp decline in American manufacturing and the loss of more than two million jobs in certain regions of the United States. Over the past two decades, the so-called China Shock has gone global, as Chinese exports have surged around the world without a comparable rise in China’s imports.
The world may soon experience the convergence of two enormous economic shocks, each reinforcing the other in terms of their direction and magnitude: The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock. The consequences of AI-driven productivity growth remain contested. But the fear is that AI will enable companies to dramatically increase output without employing more people or raising the income of ordinary citizens. The China Shock has a similar effect. China has become a dominant force in advanced manufacturing in electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, artificial intelligence, and robotic technology. But China’s growing competitiveness has led to a global surge of Chinese exports without a corresponding global surge of Chinese imports.
On top of the China Shock, the AI Productivity Shock could further widen the gap between global supply and demand, and create new economic imbalances and strains on a scale the world has not witnessed.
The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock share one critical feature: both can produce a glut of output without generating a corresponding increase in demand. In China, production has grown faster than consumption; with AI, the fear is that the technology will generate wealth without creating jobs. In both cases, the gains tend to flow to the owners of capital—and in China’s case, also to the government—rather than to workers and households.
But the iron law of economics still holds: supply requires demand, and an economy can absorb a large increase in output only if enough people have the income to buy what it produces. Economists have long described it as a problem of effective demand: the recognition that supply does not automatically create its own demand. For that to happen, greater production and supply have to translate into more jobs and higher incomes.
Whether AI will create such an imbalance is still a matter of debate. Optimists point to earlier waves of automation. Technologies such as the tractor and the spreadsheet displaced certain kinds of work but eventually helped create other kinds of work and generated jobs and additional income for workers. Only time will tell whether AI, which differs significantly from earlier technologies, will follow that pattern. What we do know is that this optimistic scenario of technological progress has yet to deliver the gains in employment and household purchasing power in China.
China is now regarded as one of the world’s leading technological powers. In some industries, China’s factories are producing more than the global demand put together. China makes more than 80% of the world’s solar panels, and its factories can turn out roughly twice as many modules in a year as the entire planet installs. In batteries, China’s manufacturing capacity is already more than double the current global demand. One projection suggests that, by 2030, China alone could produce more batteries than the whole world will use.
But China’s technological advancement is far more visible in what its factories can produce than in what its households can afford to buy and consume. Youth unemployment in the country is rising, and domestic consumption has stagnated. The unemployment rate among urban Chinese aged 16 to 24 climbed to a record 18.9 % in August 2025, according to official statistics. The real figure is likely to be much higher.
Economic progress is defined by progress in both production and consumption. These two areas of human activity move in tandem with each other and are mutually reinforcing. Faster productivity leads to rising output , which raises incomes and allows households to buy more of what is being produced. Historically, before the age of AI, this has been the case. The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock may break that connection. What made, and continues to make, the China Shock so disruptive is the immense disparity between the scale of China’s exports and its purchases from the rest of the world. China’s imports consist largely of agricultural products, minerals, and energy products that it cannot produce in sufficient quantities on its soil.
China’s exports lower prices for consumers abroad, a benefit on the expenditure side. But households need income to consume, and that income comes from the production side of the economy. But the Chinese economy is not generating a corresponding increase in income for the rest of the world by importing more from them and boosting their production. China has roughly 35% of the world’s manufacturing capacity but accounts for about just 11% of global consumption. Household consumption in the country amounts to a mere 39% of its GDP, compared with 68% in America. This imbalance is unsustainable—for both China and the world.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of Thousands Protest Cuts to Public Broadcasting
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of Thousands Protest Cuts to Public Broadcasting
articles.content_orig:
Estimated 350,000 people rally against plan to scrap licence fees and fund broadcasters from state budget
Hundreds of thousands of Czechs have rallied in Prague to protest against a perceived government attempt to stifle media freedom.
The gathering on Sunday to save the mandatory licence fees that fund Czechia’s public broadcasters drew more than 350,000 people, making it one of the biggest in the country’s history, organisers said.
Many people wore triangular paper hats similar to an animated TV character called Večerníček, a children’s bedtime story mascot who has become a symbol of the protest. Others carried banners saying: “We won’t give media away.”
The event was held at the capital’s Letná Plain, the cradle of the 1989 Velvet Revolution which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.
It marked the latest challenge to the prime minister, Andrej Babiš, and his coalition of populist, hard-right nationalist and Eurosceptic parties, and follows weeks of demonstrations in towns and cities and a strike by staff at Czech TV and Czech Radio.
Protesters say the plan to scrap licence fees and fund the broadcasters from the state budget would give ministers more leverage over newsrooms and follows the example of Hungary, Poland, Serbia and Slovakia , where current and previous rightwing populist governments eroded media independence.
A series of protests has been held since late October, when the first reading of the bill to scrap the licence fees was pushed through in the middle of the night.
The Million Moments for Democracy group, which organised the demonstration, said the authorities would now grasp the level of opposition. “We do witness here something extraordinary today,” said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organiser. “It’s just a beginning.”
In a statement, the group demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners posed a threat to democracy. “Babiš and his government obviously think they will get away with anything … that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property,” the group said.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” said one protest banner. “Hands off the media,” said another.
Šárka Dumišincová, a singer, said for her the media represented freedom. “The fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today,” she told the Associated Press.
“We need to keep media independent. The government is taking steps to control them, cut their funding and affect what they broadcast,” computer programmer Jan Snasel told AFP at the rally.
The proposed changes, which would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15%, have drawn fire from international media organisations.
The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have also criticised the government’s media plan, likening it to controversial moves by Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico , and Hungary’s former premier Viktor Orbán .
Babiš, a billionaire who returned to power last year, said protesters were riling up the public with unfounded claims about threats to media freedom.
Last week, he published an op-ed on what he called the “seven lies” being peddled by the opposition over the licence fees, which together add up to 205 koruna (£7) a month.
“Anyone who talks about ‘nationalisation’ [of public media] is deliberately lying,” he wrote, describing the criticism as “hysterical outbursts”. “Under no circumstances will we interfere in editorial work.”
Babiš heads a coalition that includes his ANO, or YES, movement, the rightwing Motorists for Themselves and the anti-migrant and pro-Russian Freedom and Direct Democracy party. Despite the protests, ANO still enjoys the backing of about 30% in opinion polls.

articles.title_orig: Bessent questions did Nvidia "goose" earnings with suspect China chip sales
articles.title_zh: Bessent questions did Nvidia "goose" earnings with suspect China chip sales
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings.
Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said in an interview on Fox News.
The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter.
Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter.
Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.
Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.
Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang.
"If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell.
Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales.
Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months.
"But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.
The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place.
Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners.
Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said.
There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information.
Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China . Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut.
Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

Labour ministers will consider calls to stagger the age of consent to make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have a sexual relationship with 16 and 17-year-olds.
The Government is set to look at demands to protect teens from sexual exploitation by older partners following allegations against Russell Brand and David Walliams .
Disgraced comedian Brand, 51, was jailed on Monday for ten-and-a-half years after his conviction for rape and sexual assault.
A woman who says she was groomed by Brand when she was 16 and he was 30 has now become the first of his accusers to waive her anonymity.
Mia Latter, 37, decided to reveal her identity to open up about the alleged abuse she suffered at Brand's hands when she was just a teenager.
It comes after a woman described an alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as 'sexual assault'.

Louise Haigh, the Prime Minister's de facto deputy, told The Sunday Times : 'It is heartbreaking to hear Mia's story.
'We need to listen to Mia and other victims like her who have been through these experiences, because it's really important that as lawmakers their experience is at the heart of what we consider.'
Ms Latter has called for the introduction of a staggered age of consent – which would make sexual relationships between adults and teenagers aged 16 and 17 illegal.
The current age of consent in the UK was set at 16 in 1885.
First Secretary of State Ms Haigh said: 'It clearly would be a massive step to change the age of consent, but it deserves proper consideration and scrutiny.
'I can absolutely understand why she is calling for it.'
Pat McFadden, the Work and Pensions Secretary, also said the Government would look at the issue.
He told Times Radio: 'I think Mia has raised an important question today.
'I'm sure it will be discussed and considered by people but I don't know what the outcome of that will be because I think there's probably a number of things to think through on this.'
The Cabinet minister added: 'I think there's a number of things to think about but what's really important is young men and women feel safe when they come to a workplace for example that they don't feel they're at the mercy of some powerful man abusing his position.
'So, those issues of age gaps may come into it, especially when someone's very young but as I say I don't have a conclusion to that question today.'
Tory work and pensions spokesman Helen Whately, who has a 16-year-old daughter, suggested it may be time to act because now you see 'so many people – and it seems to be in plain sight – going about abusing' and 'taking advantage of young women'.
Reform UK MP Danny Kruger said the 'instinct' behind a potential law change is 'clearly right' but warned it must not 'confuse us further'.
He told Times Radio: 'I'm afraid that we have a chronic reality where older men sexually preying on young girls who may be legal but are clearly very vulnerable. So I applaud the impulse.
'I worry about a complicated law that sends confusing signals about what's acceptable and what isn't. I want a culture in which it's just expected that older men don't prey on teenage girls.
'If we change the law, let's make sure it actually works and doesn't confuse us further because ultimately, culture will influence behaviour rather than the law.'
Anna Edmundson, director of policy and social change at the NSPCC, said: 'The NSPCC has long campaigned for better protections for teenagers and in 2022 helped change the law to prevent more adults in positions of trust from having sexual relationships with 16 to 17-year-olds they have power over.
'Since then, we have seen many other disturbing examples where adults appear to be targeting young people to sexually exploit them. This is completely unacceptable.
'That's why we welcome comments from Government ministers indicating a willingness to reconsider the current legal framework.
'We urgently need a review of what is and isn't working to ensure 16 and 17-year-olds are fully protected in law from this predatory behaviour.'
Brand was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and he is now serving a ten-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults.
During his trial, Brand's defence team had claimed that the women who spoke out in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, 'In Plain Sight', were actresses and even questioned whether some existed – though Ms Latter herself appeared in it as a silhouette and was given the name 'Alice'.
Brand denied all the allegations of the original investigation in 2023. Ms Latter spoke to the police after the documentary aired, but the Crown Prosecution Service decided not to include her in the trial. Officers told her they wanted her to give evidence at a potential second trial.
It was announced on Friday that a series of 'serious' sex offence allegations against Walliams are being probed by the Metropolitan Police following an investigation by The Guardian and ITV News.
One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as 'sexual assault'. He denies any wrongdoing.

articles.title_orig: Trident submarine returns home after record-breaking undersea patrol
articles.title_zh: Trident submarine returns home after record-breaking undersea patrol
articles.content_orig:
A Royal Navy submarine carrying Trident nuclear missiles has returned to its Scottish base after a record-breaking 217 days spent submerged on patrol.
The 140-strong crew of HMS Vengeance have spent the tour in almost total isolation beneath the surface after setting out from Faslane, near Helensburgh, Argyll and Bute, on 12 April.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome them home after the longest deployment at sea for a British vessel.
The typical patrol length for the UK's Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines has more than doubled in recent years, with six-month durations now routine due to a shortage of seaworthy vessels.
Crew members could be seen standing on HMS Vengeance as it travelled up Gare Loch earlier, accompanied by some smaller Naval support vessels and tug boats.
The vessel was encrusted in marine growth and some of its sound-absorbing tiles were missing.
HMS Vengeance was expected back at Faslane last weekend, but that was reported to have been delayed when the submarine replacing it on patrol had to return to base to fix a technical fault.
The head of the navy, First Sea Lord Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, praised the dedication of  submariners in keeping Nato safe at a conference last week in Oslo, but said the UK must do better at maintaining the fleet.
Streeting said it "doesn't sit lightly" with him that crews were being asked to serve longer than intended.
He said: "It makes me feel even more indebted to the crew for the service they've given to the country, for the commitment they show, the dedication, the professionalism, the expertise.
"I think the whole country can be extraordinarily proud of our submariners and of our nuclear deterrent."
Since 1969 the UK has always had at least one ballistic missile-armed submarine patrolling at sea in order to provide a "nuclear deterrent".
The logic is that if Britain was under nuclear attack, it could launch a retaliatory strike on the aggressor, a concept known as mutually-assured destruction.
The four 492ft (150m) long Vanguard-class submarines can carry up to 16 Trident missiles, each capable of delivering multiple warheads which are several times more powerful than the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima in 1945.
In order to avoid detection the submarines remain submerged and in radio silence throughout the patrol because a transmission could give away their position.
But they can ascend to shallower depths and receive encoded messages via a floating wire antenna or communications buoy.
Crews have little contact with the loved ones apart from the "Familygram" - a 120-word message that arrives weekly, and they are not permitted to reply.
Messages are vetted and bad news from home can be withheld if it might jeopardise the operational effectiveness of a crew member.
Depending on the sea state they may be able to listen to radio bulletins.
Most of the crew work in shifts of six hours on, six hours off and sleep in narrow bunks, sometimes nine to a cabin.
Submariners returning from long patrols are said to find the outside world smells strange or even overwhelming because they have become so used to filtered air.
Their distance perception could also be affected by living in such a confined space for so long and they are advised not to drive for a few days while they adjust.
The Vanguard-class boats were commissioned in the 1990s with an expected service life of 25 years but are now expected to serve for up to 40 years before the first Dreadnought-class submarines start replacing them in the early 2030s.
Streeting said that program was "on track" and that it was important to get those vessels out "as soon as possible".
Patrols used to typically last three months but in recent years this has stretched to six or more because at least one of the boats has been out of action for refit or repairs.
A major overhaul of HMS Vanguard at Devonport Dockyard in Plymouth dragged on for seven years before it returned to service in 2022.
HMS Victorious is currently in dry dock undergoing a £560m "deep maintenance" that began in 2023, leaving only Vengeance, Vigilant and Vanguard operational.
The previous record for a Royal Navy continuous undersea patrol is reported to have been set by Vanguard in April when it returned to Faslane after 205 days away.
The patrol lengths of Russian or Chinese submarines are not known, but most navies are believed to send their vessels out for far shorter durations.

articles.title_orig: Meet the miso-making engineer behind Anthropic’s biggest hit
articles.title_zh: Meet the miso-making engineer behind Anthropic’s biggest hit
articles.content_orig:
Boris Cherny loves to code. So much, in fact, that he once said coding is the reason most people choose to become engineers in the first place.
He’s also the reason why many tech workers may never have to write a line of code again.
Cherny, 35, is the creator of Claude Code, the wildly popular Anthropic coding agent that’s made the company a driving AI force. The agent can write code, run commands, and access files to accomplish work on a user’s behalf. Claude Code was a hit with programmers and non-programmers alike in Silicon Valley, giving Anthropic an early foothold in the workplace. The tool also paved the way for Anthropic’s AI tools to play a larger role in industries like finance, legal work, marketing and more.
Anthropic’s success has thrust the company into the middle of both the anxieties and optimism about AI’s impact on future jobs , and Cherny has embraced his place in that discussion.
“I think for the job market, in particular for engineers, it will be disruptive,” Cherny said in an interview with CNN earlier this year. “I hope that over the long term, it’s amazing for humanity and what it unlocks.”
Anthropic’s expected more than trillion-dollar initial public offering hinges on whether it can succeed in making Claude indispensable to office work.
And it all started with Cherny’s Claude Code.
“When people think about the IPO, they’re thinking, ‘Okay, how much room left does Claude Code have to grow?’” Willy Lee, principal at venture capital firm Neostellar, whose portfolio includes OpenAI and CoreWeave, told CNN.
Here’s how Cherny, whose official title is head of applications, became a critical part of Anthropic and the broader discourse over AI’s impact on jobs.
Cherny joined Anthropic in 2024 after a nearly seven-year run at Meta, where he worked in various divisions, including Instagram, Facebook Groups and the code quality team, according to his LinkedIn.
In 2022, during his Meta tenure, he and his wife temporarily moved to Japan for her work. Across the world from his colleagues in California, Cherny loved being able to code all day without the interruptions of meetings and project management tasks, he said on an episode of the tech industry podcast “The Peterman Pod” in 2025.
He was one of the few engineers in Meta’s Instagram division who was coding so much.
“For me, when I write code, I have an emotional relationship with it, and it’s something I think about when I’m really deep in a problem,” he said on the podcast. “I dream about it.”
He spent a month experimenting with Anthropic’s models after joining the company, he told “ Lenny’s Podcast, ” a show about product development. In his early days at Anthropic, he mostly built prototypes to test the boundaries of what the Claude maker’s AI could do.
But he reached a turning point a couple of months later when he created a command-line interface tool for Claude, which enabled the AI helper to interact directly with his computer’s operating system. Cherny made a simple request: figure out what music he was listening to.
He was shocked when the tool wrote code to answer that question without being specifically told to do so.
“The model was given this tool, and it figured out how to use it to answer this question that I had that I wasn’t even sure it could answer,” he said on “Lenny’s Podcast.”
That side project laid the foundation for Claude Code, which surpassed $2.5 billion in run-rate revenue in February. Anthropic doesn’t disclose usage numbers for Claude Code, but a chart in the company’s S-1 filing ahead of its IPO shows revenue ramping up following Claude Code’s release.
For Cherny, expanding Claude Code’s reach involves talking to real people about how they use the product. On X, Cherny replies to questions from Claude users on a weekly — sometimes almost daily — basis.
It’s a habit he formed long before joining Anthropic. When he worked at Meta in California, he often showed the cafeteria workers new features to see if they were able to figure them out quickly, he told “The Peterman Pod.”
“The thing that actually excites me is talking to people and understanding how we can make the product better,” he told CNN in March. “I’m just completely focused on that.”
Enterprise AI spending accelerated in late 2025 following Claude Code’s release to the general public in May, said Ara Kharazian, senior economist at financial services company Ramp, which tracks business spending on AI.
“That was the first commercially advanced version of AI that was directly productivity enhancing for a specific segment of jobs,” he said of Claude Code and other coding agents.
Anthropic’s coding tool served as a jumping-off point for Claude Cowork, the company’s AI agent for general office work that can manage files and automate tasks. The idea for Cowork came after Cherny observed people and companies using Claude Code for non-technical duties. Cherny himself uses it for paying parking tickets and project management work for his team at Anthropic, he said on “Lenny’s Podcast.”
Non-technical employees at the Mid-Ohio Food Collective frequently use Claude Code, according to Mark Mollenkopf, the organization’s director of software engineering. Its director of nutrition used Claude Code to build a game that’s like Tinder for food, aiming to help families choose healthier options based on their preferences.
They had the idea for nearly a decade; Mollenkopf says he still has photos of a whiteboard with the initial concept from 2017. But the team has been too busy with higher priority tasks until it’s been able to have Claude Code handle it.
“We’re not going to put it in production today yet, but it’s that unlock for us to be able to democratize great ideas that we’ve always had,” Mollenkopf said.
Anthropic built Claude Cowork in 10 days using Claude Code. It shows how important Cherny’s brainchild has been for Anthropic’s own growth, not just drawing in more customers.
Still, the company faces myriad challenges, including increased competition from OpenAI, reliance on a limited number of customers and pressure to live up to its sky-high valuation.
Meanwhile, Anthropic has played a fundamental yet complicated role in the AI boom.
The company has warned about the risks of AI, saying it’s capable of catastrophic consequences , yet it continues to charge ahead with new models. It worries that the economy isn’t ready for AI’s impact on jobs, yet it creates and iterates on tools like Claude Code and Claude Cowork for automating work.
Cherny is at the center of that paradox. Some software engineers have grown increasingly wary of AI’s role in their jobs, with six in 10 tech workers saying they actively try to avoid using AI , according to a recent survey of 30,000 programmers conducted by tech site Stack Overflow. Some believe the tech isn’t as capable as it’s been made out to be, while others feel AI’s role in tech has led to more burnout over the pressure to perform and stay up to date on the newest technologies.
Cherny has a lot of thoughts about what the future looks like. The job of a software engineer already involves doing a lot more than just coding; it entails working with designers and other teams, and figuring out what to build next. As AI takes over most coding tasks, engineers will be freed up to focus on these other parts of the job, he said.
That’s why he said in March that he thinks software engineering jobs are going to start disappearing by the end of this year.
“The (job) title will be maybe ‘builder,’” he told CNN. “Maybe we’ll still call them software engineers, but they’re going to do much more than engineers do today.”
Cherny has emerged as somewhat of an icon among developers and engineers like Mollenkopf, who said he watches podcasts featuring the Claude Code creator and others in similar roles to learn more about AI. That’s how Mollenkopf learned about Claude Tag, a feature that lets users connect work data to Claude and then tag the AI helper in Slack.

articles.title_orig: How Jensen Huang Built a Business to Feed Chinese Appetite for American Chips
articles.title_zh: How Jensen Huang Built a Business to Feed Chinese Appetite for American Chips
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Over three decades, Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang helped propel the chipmaker’s rise into one of the world’s most valuable and resilient companies, leading the business through near-death and periods of reinvention.
Now the self-described “battlefield CEO” faces a personal crisis that will test a roughly $4-trillion Silicon Valley powerhouse that has become the face of the artificial intelligence revolution.
Over the weekend, the 63-year-old tech billionaire and married father of two sent an apology to his employees, admitting he had an affair and is hoping to win back trust. Nvidia’s board announced it is launching an investigation after allegations surfaced that Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
“Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence,” Huang said in the note to employees.
The board said it doesn’t believe the relationship compromised Nvidia’s secrets or national security. China has dismissed the allegations as an unsubstantiated “smear” campaign against the country.
The revelations, though, rattled Silicon Valley and Washington, where federal lawmakers have called for an investigation into accusations that China targeted the powerful tech mogul. The scandal also comes as the U.S. competes with China in the AI race, raising more scrutiny over Nvidia’s business with the country.
Nvidia launched the investigation after the New York Times first reported in late October that American intelligence agencies found that Huang developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen that was passing on intelligence to Beijing. The woman, Alice Huang, worked as an executive for Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which is one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed didn’t respond to a request for comment but told the New York Times that it “cannot respond to a media trial and welcomes formal, evidence-based investigation.”
On Monday, Nvidia’s share price fell about 5% to roughly $177  as investors expressed anxiety about how the scandal will affect the company’s future.
Though analysts say it’s unlikely that Huang will be ousted as chief executive and Nvidia will probably remain a dominant AI player, the drama has raised questions about the company’s succession plans and how it will affect the chipmaker’s competition with rivals.
“He’s become a tech celebrity, which has shown to be both a blessing and a curse for companies. His conduct could raise questions about his judgment and potentially undermine some of the confidence he’s built among investors, customers and developers,” said Jacob Bourne, an eMarketer analyst.
Over the years, Huang, who’s known for donning a black leather jacket, has shown he’s a visionary, dealmaker and politically savvy, forging strong ties with President Trump. Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at Technalysis Research, said that Nvidia will likely be around for decades, but that the scandal is shining a spotlight on who will succeed Huang.
That will be hard to top. Huang’s two children work for Nvidia.
“He’s been able to turn that big personality and vision and dealmaking into this point where he is arguably the leader, certainly of the hardware side of the tech industry,” O’Donnell said. “Everything he says matters and every company wants to do deals with Nvidia.”
Huang is no stranger to navigating through turmoil, and as a leader he’s emphasized the importance of character and resilience.
Born in Taiwan, Huang spent some time in Thailand before his family sent him to the United States, where he attended a religious reform school. There, he told news outlets, he was bullied for being Chinese and even scrubbed toilets.
He met his future wife, Lori, at Oregon State University, where they were studying electrical engineering.
Huang, along with engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, founded Nvidia in 1993 at a Denny’s diner in San José,  where they envisioned building a computer chip to improve video game graphics.
In its early days, Nvidia contracted with game company Sega, but it almost went out of business by betting on the wrong approach for building graphics chips. Huang laid off employees and convinced Sega to invest $5 million in the company, avoiding bankruptcy, according to an interview he did on “How I Built This with Guy Raz.”
The company created specialized computer chips that would not only be used for gaming but also for cryptocurrency mining, AI model training and robotics.
Nvidia also partnered with OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, early, before people turned more to AI to automate tasks. In 2016, Huang hand-delivered Nvidia’s new supercomputer to OpenAI. As ChatGPT became more popular, Nvidia benefited from the AI boom.
“He’s been on the cutting edge of all of this for a very long time, and then the rest of the world kind of caught up with what he saw and what the industry was doing, and now of course we are where we are,” O’Donnell said.
As other tech leaders have called for a slowdown of the AI race, Huang has called for speeding up AI innovation, stating it could help improve safety. Computers, he said, are just software and not conscious.
Even as Nvidia’s prominence has grown, Huang has told media outlets he still worries the company could go out of business, though he says he’s stepped up in times of crisis.
“The perfect day is [when] we are in trouble, and you just create the worst possible condition. And Jensen, we need you to come and help us think through this,” Huang said in an interview on “How I Built This with Guy Raz.”
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: UPS plane, Copa Airlines flight collide on taxiway at Miami International Airport - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Two people were treated for minor injuries, airport officials said.
A UPS cargo plane and a Copa Airlines passenger jet collided on a taxiway at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, according to airport officials and the Federal Aviation Administration.
Two people were treated at the scene for minor injuries by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue, but did not need to be taken to the hospital, according to Miami-Dade Aviation.
Six crew members and 166 passengers were on the Copa aircraft -- a Boeing 737-800NG -- and, aside from the two who were treated for "apparent minor injuries," all the other passengers crew members "are reported to be in good condition," the airline said in a statement.
"Preliminary information indicates that a cargo aircraft and the left wingtip of the Copa Airlines aircraft came into contact while both aircraft were taxiing," the airline said. "Copa Airlines regrets the disruption this incident may cause our passengers. The safety of our passengers and crew is our top priority, and we will cooperate with authorities as they investigate the incident."
The collision happened at approximately 9:15 p.m., the airport said.
The wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737, which was taxiing to the gate, struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767, which was taxiing for departure to Bogota, Colombia, according to a statement from the FAA. The FAA said it is investigating the incident.
Air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight, the FAA said. One pilot is heard on air traffic controller audio saying, "Somebody hit us." Photos showed damage to the nose of one of the planes.
The airport said flights were being directed to other taxiways, so there was no impact to airport operations.
"We are aware of an incident involving one of our aircraft on the ground in Miami," UPS said in a statement. "Our crew is safe, and we are committed to working with authorities to determine what happened. The safety of our employees and the public is our highest priority."

articles.title_zh: Estonia to shut its border with Russia, blaming Moscow for foiled arson plot
articles.content_orig:
Estonia is to close its border with Russia after blaming Moscow for a suspected attack on a defense technology company, Estonia’s prime minister said Sunday.
Eight people have been detained after allegedly attempting an arson attack on the company overnight on Saturday, authorities say. No one was injured.
Estonian security services say the attempted attack was carried out on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU.
“If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face,” Prime Minister Kristen Michal said in a statement Sunday.
“Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defense industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable,” he added.
Border crossings will be closed from December 1, and Michal did not say when they would reopen.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Russian state news agency TASS that the move is part of a wider pattern of “Russophobia.”
“We’ll check all this for veracity,” Zakharova said. “But if these are their real plans, then they’re part of another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia.”
Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the “attempted sabotage” this weekend was “yet another reminder that Russia’s hostile activities extend far beyond Ukraine” and that “hostile actions must have consequences.” He said he expected further sanctions to be adopted targeting Russian individuals and entities at a meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Brussels, Belgium on Monday.
Ukraine has commended Estonia for its move to close the border, hailing it as an example of effective action against Russian hostility and encouraging Europe to take note.
“Estonia has shown that Russian sabotage can and should have consequences beyond diplomatic condemnation,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X . “This approach deserves wider support across Europe.”
Russia has long been accused of carrying out sabotage and other hybrid attacks against Europe but has repeatedly denied the claims.
Russia is escalating its attacks on Europe. The risk of a misstep is growing every day
Back in September, European officials pointed the finger at the Kremlin following a series of incidents that appeared to target NATO members.
A railway line on which several former Western diplomats were traveling was struck by a Russian drone near Ukraine’s border with Poland, while another drone – likely of Russian origin – was shot down in Lithuania. A third drone also washed ashore in Poland.
Elsewhere, a Danish helicopter was narrowly missed by a Russian flare, and Dutch rail traffic was significantly disrupted after metal pipes that had been fitted across the tracks triggered short circuits, turned traffic signals to red and forced trains to an inconvenient stop.
Despite denying involvement, Moscow has remained the alleged culprit. European NATO-member allies have deemed the actions an escalation of conflict against the bloc – characterizing the attacks as measures designed to antagonize without triggering all-out war.

articles.title_orig: Army whistleblower alleges senior military officials ignored warnings ahead of deadly attack in Kuwait
articles.title_zh: Army whistleblower alleges senior military officials ignored warnings ahead of deadly attack in Kuwait
articles.content_orig:
A U.S. Army soldier who survived a deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran .
The whistleblower, Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, spoke exclusively with 60 Minutes ' Norah O'Donnell about his complaint, which was submitted to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Friday and obtained by CBS News.
He alleges Army leaders dismissed concerns over thin fortifications at a U.S. command post in Kuwait where six American soldiers were killed by an Iranian drone in the first 24 hours of the conflict, the deadliest attack on U.S. troops in the war.
The complaint also claims the post — known as Port Shuaiba — "had no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance."
"I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself — all the way down to my level," Maj. Ramsbottom told 60 Minutes. "We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn."
Ramsbottom spoke with 60 Minutes as part of an eight-month investigation into the March 1 attack at the command post, known as Port Shuaiba. The day after the attack, in a press conference, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth insisted the troops there were well protected.
"Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately, we call it a squirter that makes its way through," Hegseth said. "And in that particular case it happened to hit a tactical operations center that was fortified. But these are powerful weapons."
The eyewitness accounts, along with photos and videos of the attack's aftermath, offer a staggering look at the thinly fortified Kuwaiti port facility when it was hit one day after the U.S. and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat from Connecticut and the ranking member on the Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, issued a series of demands to Hegseth after reviewing the whistleblower complaint.
In a letter dated Nov. 15, the senator called on Hegseth to appear in a classified briefing and provide "all force protection assessments" for Port Shuaiba. Democrats have signaled they will probe the administration's handling of the war with Iran when they retake both houses of Congress next year.
"The families of the six fallen servicemembers, the wounded survivors, and the American people deserve transparency and accountability," wrote Blumenthal.
A Pentagon spokesperson declined to comment on Ramsbottom's allegations, including on whether adequate force protection was in place at Port Shuaiba.

articles.title_orig: Echoes of 1989 on Letná: Prague protest largest since Velvet Revolution
articles.title_zh: Echoes of 1989 on Letná: Prague protest largest since Velvet Revolution
articles.content_orig:
Czech flags, calls to protect independent institutions and a vast crowd on Letná: two days before the Velvet Revolution anniversary, Prague’s best-known protest ground is again the setting for a demonstration with potentially historic numbers.
Between 350,000 and 450,000 people have attended Sunday’s rally in support of public-service media, according to Mikuláš Minář, chairman of organizing group Milion chvilek. If confirmed, that would make it the largest demonstration in Czechia since the revolutionary gatherings of late 1989.
That remains an organizer’s estimate. Prague police spokesperson Eva Kropáčová told Czech News Agency that police would not publish an estimated count, leaving the precise size, and any record claim, officially unverified.
The protest’s name, “Letná against 4:36,” refers to the early-morning parliamentary vote on Oct. 24 that advanced legislation changing how Czech Television and Czech Radio are financed.
The proposal would replace license-fee funding with money from the state budget. Opponents fear this could make the broadcasters more vulnerable to political pressure. Prime Minister Andrej Babiš and other coalition politicians reject those concerns and deny seeking political control.
The bill has advanced to its second reading; it has not completed the legislative process.
For organizers, the dispute also concerns how the government exercises power. Minář criticized legislation being pushed through hurriedly, overnight and without sufficient discussion. Participants responded with chants of “We care,” while signs included “We won’t give up the media.”
Representatives of students, journalism, theater, business, churches and sport have been taking turns onstage. According to organizers, all designated sectors filled shortly after the rally began, with participants also standing in the adjoining park.
Letná carries an obvious historical association. On Nov. 25, 1989, approximately 750,000 people gathered there during the Velvet Revolution, according to the Institute for the Study of Totalitarian Regimes . More than half a million returned the following day.
Sunday’s estimated attendance remains below those revolutionary crowds, but its potential significance lies in the comparison with demonstrations since the fall of communism.
Contemporary reporting records the differing 2019 estimates , while police estimated approximately 70,000 at the September 2022 protest. Organizers put this March’s Letná rally at about a quarter of a million.
Even the lower end of today’s organizer estimate exceeds the widely reported figures for both major 2019 Letná rallies.
English Prague • CZK 70,000 - 130,000
English Czech Chinese Remote work - Czechia
The proximity to Nov. 17 gives Sunday’s gathering additional resonance. In 1989, mass demonstrations helped end communist one-party rule. Today’s participants are protesting decisions by an elected government within a democratic system.
The connection is therefore one of place, timing and the defense of institutions—not an equivalence between the two political situations.
Public broadcasting also gives the anniversary a particular relevance: the argument concerns whether institutions intended to serve the public can retain sufficient independence from those holding power.
Minář has urged demonstrators to remain peaceful and report provocations to police or anti-conflict teams. By around 4:30 p.m., police had reported no major problems.
Milion chvilek is demanding withdrawal of the media-funding bill, an apology for the overnight parliamentary proceedings and substantive public discussion about the broadcasters’ future.
Its demands extend to removing Tomio Okamura as parliamentary speaker and taking the Defense Ministry away from SPD. The group accuses SPD of undermining national security.
Minář has invited the government to a public debate at Švandovo divadlo on Dec. 2 at 7 p.m. He also announced a nationwide warning action for 4:36 p.m. that day.
For Prague residents, the immediate impact is transport disruption. Police say traffic on Milady Horákové and access to the Blanka tunnel will be significantly restricted as participants leave, although trams will continue running.
The demonstration was expected to finish around 4:30 p.m. Its final attendance and the government’s response remained unresolved at the time of writing. Reporting reflects information available at 4:30 p.m. on Nov. 15, while the demonstration was ongoing; we will update as more data is made available.

articles.title_zh: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
articles.content_orig:
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the  company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
